utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Novakovic. May I remind you of the affirmation you took yesterday, which still applies. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we begin, my learned colleague of the Prosecution came to see me, and she said she had one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's not necessary any more. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now? Can you hear the English channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now yes. Not at the beginning. Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, during yesterday's examination, you mentioned the military naval sector of Kumbor. Do you know the exact name and title of that military naval sector?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I realised that there was a 9, the figure 9, so it was the 9th Military Naval Sector. I didn't know that until yesterday. We called it the Military Naval Sector of Boka, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Now, linked to the military naval sector, can you tell us what there is at Kumbor, linked to the military naval sector?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the navy, naval unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know where the command of the military naval sector is located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command is located at Kumbor, and there was another command in Zelenika, just in front of the tunnel. Now who was where, I'm not quite sure, but in Kumbor and in Zelenika. That was where the two command headquarters of the navy were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: Do you know of any other command post of the military naval sector?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning. These matters didn't arise in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to not be able to agree to you, Ms. Mahindaratne. You were asking questions about the radio communication network of this body, and I think it fairly arises. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, on the territory of the broader region around Dubrovnik, did you hear of the existence of any other command post for the VPS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, as the front drew closer to Dubrovnik, there was one in Kupari, a command post at Kupari, at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You mentioned yesterday during your testimony that on the 6th of December you started out from Herceg-Novi and that you took the road from Brgat to Zarkovica to Bosanka in order to arrive at Bosanka. Now, was that the usual, customary route that you would take to reach Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the usual, shortest route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The soldier Marko Komarica, can you tell me which unit he belonged to? Who was his commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a soldier of the 3rd Battalion, and his commander was Vladimir Kovacevic, nicknamed Rambo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Tell me, please: In that unit, the one that Marko Komarica was a regular soldier in, you, when you came to Bosanka, saw other soldiers as well, did you not, from that unit, the one belonging to -- the one that Marko Komarica belonged to? And you said, I believe, that there were a lot of soldiers from Herzegovina in that unit. Do you know which places they actually came from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was people -- there were people from Trebinje, Bileca, and Gacko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Are they inhabitants of that town, of those towns who were mobilised and belonged to this 3rd Battalion that Marko Komarica served under?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, but I never investigated matters of that kind. I didn't give it much thought, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, tell me: The people from the territory of Trebinje, Gacko, Bileca and so on, those soldiers who were from those parts, can you give one name to them? Do they come under one name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called them the men from Herzegovina, Herzegovci by virtue of the territory they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: So in the 3rd Battalion, there were quite a lot of soldiers from Herzegovina. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that they were Strugar's men, if I heard you correctly. That was the term you used when asked by my learned colleague. Can you tell me how you deduced that? How do you link those soldiers, those men were Herzegovina who were in the 3rd Battalion to General Strugar? How did you come to make that connection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that unit, the 3rd Battalion, came under the composition of the units commanded by General Strugar, but those units were, I would say, on our terrain. And as I saw that frigate captain Jovo Drljan was communicating with those units I heard a conversation with Admiral Zec and Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, nicknamed Rambo, I wasn't quite sure whether they were up there or down here. So I came to realise later, or rather, I came to realise that they were members of the 3rd Battalion, in fact belonging to the 2nd Army under the command of General Strugar, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know the exact name of that establishment, of the military Superior Command, both the Superior Command to your unit and the 9th VPS and that 3rd Battalion, whose commander was Vladimir Kovacevic? Do you know the exact name of the topmost, highest command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The highest command was the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that its name exactly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, I'm an ordinary soldier. I can be wrong on some of the names and titles. I wasn't interested in details like that. And like yesterday, November 8th, 9th, 10th, I can tell you all the details and specifics about those days because I lived through them, I experienced them. But I can't speak as precisely about these other matters because I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you mentioned that on the 5th, that is to say, talking to Komarica, I think you mentioned, connected to the 5th of December, frigate captain Zec, whom you said was up at the positions of the 3rd Battalion on the 6th of December, you saw frigate Captain Jovo Drljan, I believe, at the positions of the 3rd Battalion, and on the 7th of December, you said that you heard the voice of warship Captain Zec at the command post of the 3rd Battalion at Brgat.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Warship Captain Zec and frigate Captain Jovo Drljan, those two men, what command did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belonged to the military naval sector, the 9th one as it is professionally called, and it belonged to Kumbor and Boka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: How come you know that your unit of the Territorial Defence within the composition of the 9th -- was within the composition of the 9th Military Naval Sector? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that because my TO commander Ilija Martinovic would always go to meetings with the warship Captain Djurovic and later on Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any other unit within the composition of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just like the TO of Herceg-Novi, the one I mentioned a moment ago, there was the TO of Kotor, the TO of Budva, the TO of Bar. So that I considered that all these from Montenegro were connected and linked to that 9th Military Naval Sector, Kumbor, whereas the others were linked to Trebinje, Rambo's 3rd Battalion, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: So you thought that the 3rd Battalion, commanded by Vladimir Kovacevic, was linked to Trebinje. Now, did you think that because within the composition of that battalion, did you think along those lines because you saw that the men in those battalions were mostly from Herzegovina, there were a lot of soldiers from Trebinje, Gacko, and Bileca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was about to object because the learned counsel was leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've done it now, Mr. Rodic. Move on and don't keep doing it, I think is the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Novakovic, Colonel Jovanovic was mentioned, with the nickname Kurd, and you said that you had personal contacts, that is to say, that you saw the man, not to say close up, but anyway you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Where was the colonel from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not from Kumbor. He came from some other unit, but I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was from Montenegro or from Serbia where he came from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somebody said I think that he had come from Serbia, but somebody else said, no, he's from Podgorica. So most probably he was in fact from Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not cross-examine the witness on Colonel Jovanovic at all yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't remember any such cross-examination. Do you, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleague asked a number of questions mentioning Colonel Jovanovic, nicknamed Kurd, with that nickname, so perhaps that might remind us that we did in fact mention him yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Your Honour, and I say that with a sense of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I remember the name from yesterday, Mr. Rodic, but not in the course of cross-examination. I can't pretend to have a full recollection of that matter, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do believe that during my examination-in-chief, and then later, when my colleague asked a question from the Prosecution with respect to the pulling out of the killed and wounded at Bosanka and how they came to be killed and wounded, that that colonel, Colonel Jovanovic, nicknamed Kurd, took them on that assignment. If that can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, Mr. Rodic, I don't see that the line of re-examination that you're following is justified by the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then I'm finished with my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Novakovic, thank you very much for your coming to assist us here and for the evidence you've given. The course of your evidence is now completed, so that you are free to return to your home. Thank you very much. You may leave the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your next witness, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to call witness Milan Pavicic to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the court officer please -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pavicic. Would you please take the card and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pavicic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: First could you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I am Milan Pavicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavicic, could you please tell us where you live.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I live in Bileca, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which schools you completed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I completed the elementary school in Dubrovnik in 1975. After that, I completed the military high school in Belgrade in 1979. And in 1983, I completed the military academy in Belgrade, the land forces infantry department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you work now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm working in Bileca, in the Army of Republika Srpska, and I am the deputy commander of the school for non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work when you completed the military academy up to 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I worked in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Also in the school of reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At some point were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I was transferred from Bileca to the Trebinje garrison, to the 472nd Motorised Brigade, on the 15th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us why you were transferred, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Already in 1991, the reserve officers school was reorganised. Its numbers were reduced because of the events that were happening in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So there was a need for a number of the officers by the new establishment who were a surplus to be transferred. We were given the opportunity to choose between Sarajevo, Mostar, or Trebinje. I decided for the -- to go to the Trebinje garrison because it was close to the place where I was already working.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us: In your personal file, as far as the order of appointment, what does it state for that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The order of the 15th of September states: Order of the commander of the navy. I am being assigned as a commander of a mortar company in the 472nd Motorised Battalion in the military naval department or sector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number of the military post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat once again, since it is not in the transcript, everything that you said.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order of the commander of the navy. He wrote the order. In it, it states that I was assigned as commander of a mortar unit in the 1st Motorised Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade of the 9th Military Naval Sector or the Military Naval District.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify, because unfortunately the transcript again is not correct. But please, could you please more slowly and then you can tell me whether I understood you properly. So the 1st Motorised Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, which is part of the 9th Military Naval District, part of the military naval sector, the VPO.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether -- until what period it says in your personal files you served in the 472nd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The order of the 15th of September, 1991 was enforced up until the time I left this area, to the command of the 2nd Army on the 8th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for asking this question several times, but unfortunately in the transcript we don't see the gist of our question. I don't know the reason. The answer is not being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what I'm asking and what the witness has said several times in B/C/S is that he was deployed to the 1st Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, which was part of the 9th VPS, which is part of the naval military district. So is it correct what I have just told you, Mr. Pavicic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your battalion, your brigade, in the same composition, was that situation unchanged until 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. As far as the battalion and the brigade, it's true. However, in the meantime, the brigade was practically taken out of the composition of the 9th Military Naval Sector and came under the command of the 2nd Corps. To be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will talk about that. What I am interested in is the following: You personally, as an officer, from September 15th until 1992, until June 1992, were you personally part of the 9th Military Naval Sector or the naval military district?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us to which duties were you transferred to in the 1st Battalion of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I was transferred as commander of a mortar company, 120-millimetre mortar company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what kind of a unit was the 1st Battalion of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please tell me what you mean, what kind of a unit, when you say that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it a unit that was permanently staffed or was it a so-called R unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I understand. First of all, each unit and even brigade had a live unit which had a permanent composition. The 1st Battalion, however, had -- it was an R unit, a reserve composition, and it only had the organs of command, or part of the officers for command for development, who were there to man the unit based on mobilisation plans and so on. Specifically, the 1st Battalion was completely mobilised. It was formed anew.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: In the usual course of things, how was this unit that we're talking about manned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: This unit, and all other R composition units, based on mobilisation plans which were prepared in advance, would be manned by conscripts from the reserves, depending on where the unit was located, specifically, the 1st Battalion of the 472nd Brigade should have been staffed from the Dubrovnik-Trebinje locations and perhaps some other places in the close vicinity. In view of certain circumstances, this could not happen as it was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the brigade, or the 1st Battalion, were there any problems to staff your specific unit in accordance with the mobilisation plans?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were many problems, in view of the fact that there was only some officers for the development of the unit, and this number was not what it should have been in order to mobilise a battalion. So besides those officers, there weren't enough conscripts either within certain units, within the battalion, the units were not manned adequately up to the percentage that was required in order to implement any tasks. So these are the problems in brief. If we keep in mind that besides this specific problem, we also had problems with the logistic support and all the other problems that came with that, then you will see for yourself that there were very many problems while implementing the mobilisation of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened? Why was your battalion not mobilised from the composition of those people who had their combat assignments as part of the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: What I found out as soon as I arrived there, since we were in the process of forming the unit, some conscripts were either from Dubrovnik or Trebinje or were of other ethnic groups, which was a sensitive issue when we were talking about the manning of this and other units. A lot of people did not respond to the mobilisation call. This applied to this unit as well. So what I knew was that the percentage in those initial days, the way we calculate that, how much time is required to mobilise a certain unit, this figure came to 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since the unit could not be fully manned by reserves who had their wartime assignments in that unit, how did you staff those units? Which personnel did you use?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: At the time, this battalion was filled with active soldiers, young soldiers, who were serving their regular military duty, and they came from other places. So because there were so many of them, I could not tell you which were the places that they came from, but they were in the process -- or they were undergoing training at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: How did the fact that a large number of officers were -- new officers were arriving who were never in that unit, how did that fact reflect on the work and the readiness of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Since the majority of the units that were being mobilised had people who knew each other, and we're talking about soldiers, this happened to be a unit where the majority of officers and soldiers, both active and reserve ones, simply didn't know one another, the people didn't know each other, the officers didn't know each other. So all the problems stemmed from that fact and led to a number of problems in terms of organising the life, the work, preparation for the implementation of certain tasks. So there were a lot of problems, and it took some time for the unit to begin to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: How much time passed from the time that you came to the unit before this unit actually was deployed to its positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The unit was set up on the 15th, as soon as I arrived in Trebinje, and already by the 19th we had taken up our firing positions. We had taken up the positions that we were ordered to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say the 15th and the 19th, which month are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of September. September 15th and September 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak more slowly and could we pause between my question and your answer so that everything that we are saying can be recorded in the transcript. Thank you. Tell me: Were there any problems in respect of having the units act in concert, units that were in different positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Specifically, first of all, at first, we did not know which units were on the left and which units were on the right. So the organisation of action in concert was not done according to the rules. And also, within the unit, due to the above-mentioned problems, there were additional difficulties in terms of coordination, action in concert, et cetera, and this particularly came to the fore later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was commander of the 472nd Motorised Brigade until September?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. Until the 19th of September, it was Lieutenant Colonel Nojko Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened with Mr. Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of September, Nojko Marinovic went to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "went to Dubrovnik," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, he expressed the wish not to belong to the JNA any longer. Part of his officers and soldiers packed his belongings and without any problems whatsoever, he went to Dubrovnik. They said goodbye. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This fact that the commander left the unit, how did it affect the personnel of the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: It affected them very badly. The very knowledge that the commander left the unit, regardless of the fact that he left under normal conditions, if we can put it that way, nevertheless had a negative affect on the general feeling amongst the officers and soldiers. It was believed that since he had left, he would tell the other side everything about the brigade, the firing positions of the artillery pieces, the deployment, everything that had to do with the brigade. So at any rate, it had a very negative effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, if you know, within which bigger formation in the period from September until December 1991 the 472nd Brigade was, and were there any changes? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the brigade was, in terms of establishment, until I came there, was within the 9th Military Naval Sector. So that is that part. Later on, it became part of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Later on, were there any other changes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, later. Since it was within the composition of the 9th Military Naval District before, it was returned to its composition yet again. I can't remember exactly when, but it was the end of October, or rather, already by the end of November, it became part of the 2nd Corps. Now, was this the end of November? I think so. I think it was the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what unit the 472nd Motorised Brigade originally belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: When you say "originally," what period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to its original establishment throughout the period that we are discussing here, excluding the period before the re-subordination of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: It was originally within the 9th Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us a few minutes ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we clarify one particular matter. Original unit, the original unit that this unit belonged to is the 9th Military Naval Sector, and from the 9th Military Naval Sector, the unit was temporarily re-subordinated and attached elsewhere. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. That clearly was the case, Mr. Petrovic. Would you move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the transcript - I don't know why - but the transcript is not reflecting what the witness is saying. We are going to ask for the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you ask the witness to repeat his evidence rather than you giving it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavicic, the original unit, what is the original unit that the 472nd Motorised Brigade belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The 472nd Motorised Brigade belonged to the 9th Military Naval Sector. But let me clarify straight away what I know. It was always within that composition, until it became part of the 2nd Operational Group. So this was September or October. I think it was by the end of October. After that, it was returned yet again to its original establishment, that is to say, the 9th Military Naval Sector. So this is approximately the end of November, and then it became part of the 2nd Corps. So several times it went outside its original establishment. First it was within the 9th VPS, then the operational group, then the 9th VPS again, and then the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What positions did your unit take on this 19th of September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the unit that I commanded, that is to say, the 1st Mortar Company, was within the area of Zaplanik. That's where its positions were. And the other units of the 1st Battalion took up the facilities along the border with Croatia. The objective was to stop possible attacks from the Croatian side within the area of responsibility of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the toponyms where your battalion was deployed? What are the names of those places?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Golubov Kamen, Ostra Glava, Velika Gomila, Velika Zedj and in depth Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For how long was your unit at those positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: My unit, and therefore the entire battalion, were at these positions until the end of November, that is to say, the 28th of November, 1991, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document P124. This is a map which was exhibited during the evidence of Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavicic, please look at this map. But I would like to ask you to try to look at the ELMO and to point out the area where the deployment of your battalion can be seen. So the map should only be moved a bit up.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please move the map a bit further up so that we could see this area. Yes, that's right. And could we zoom this in a bit. A bit more. Fine. Thank you. Mr. Pavicic, can you show us on this map, on the ELMO, can you use the pointer and show us -- could you please use the pointer on the ELMO itself and tell us where your battalion was.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us the names of the places.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: It's from here. It is this area, this area is marked properly. This is where the command was. This is where my firing position was. And this is the area. This is the area of the battalion. I don't know if you need it in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That will suffice. Could you please be so kind as to tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You can leave the map on the ELMO, please. You can leave it there, because we need it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us clarify this once again. From when was your unit at these positions that are marked on this map, and until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: From the 19th of September until the 28th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us: In this first period, do you know for what reason your unit was deployed in the area that we saw on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: What I know and what I was tasked by my superior officer to do was, specifically, to take positions, or rather, vital facilities along the border with Croatia, and not to allow a possible breakthrough by Croatian forces deep into the territory, or rather, within the area of responsibility of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this first period, the period of September 1991, were there any actions, or rather, provocations, from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was sporadic action by infantry weapons, especially on our left flank. Further on, this was mostly from the area of Komolac, Bosanka, Brgat, that area. So there were provocations from infantry weapons at first, especially against our left flank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps whether there were any casualties on your side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Not in the unit that I was in. However, later I heard that the first casualty was on the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what this was about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: There was sporadic gunfire at this left flank, so this was infantry gunfire, and this is the first casualty in the Trebinje area, as far as I know, and this was specifically on the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "casualty," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the killing of one of our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at that time who was on the other side? Who was it who was carrying out these provocations? Who opened gunfire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: These are Croatian forces. Which specific units these were, I don't know, and I don't know what the strength of these units was, but it was the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this period that we are talking about, do you know where the positions were of the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: In this period, what I could note from the observation post, that is to say, the sporadic gunfire, these provocations came from -- now, well, this is 326, Strincijera, and now I can't remember the name any longer, but this is -- this area, Bosanka, Dubrava, Gradci, that broader area. It is barely discernible in this map. If it were a larger-scale map I could point it out more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you just show us on the map itself where these positions are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: 326 is approximately -- I'm sorry. It's this area here. Strincijera is here, approximately, then Dubrava, here, in this area, and Gradic [phoen]. This is practically the area. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in this initial period, when were the forces from the other side there? In which period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: In fact, as soon as we got there on the 19th or 20th, when we took up this position, sporadic gunfire already started, and as time went by, their action became more intensive. So this was infantry weapons for the most part in this first period, these first 10 or 15 days, until the end of September, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did your unit first open gunfire at the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Specifically, my unit, or rather, the unit I commanded, opened fire on the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were your targets?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Golubov Kamen, Ostra Glava, and Velika Gomila specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us the following: The Croatian side, what kind of weapons did it have in that first period, September, October, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I've already said towards the end of September. By the end of September, it was mostly infantry weapons and that is the kind of gunfire that we managed to note. However, from the 1st onwards, they started using mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, specifically. Among other things, one of these projectiles was fired at my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Later on, did the Croatian side obtain other weapons too?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm saying specifically what I managed to see. At first, there were 82-millimetre mortars, and later on, already in November, the beginning of November, they included 120-millimetre-calibre weapons, specifically in this area where our battalion was. This is classical weapons. However, there were other things there too, as far as we managed to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me ask you something. In that period, did you see any weapons of the Croatian side that were mounted on motor vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I saw for the first time then. We called this Charlie. I don't know why it was called Charlie, but that's what we called it. Why we called this weapon Charlie, I don't know. Actually, this is a mortar mounted on a motor vehicle, on a Zastava, a well-known motor vehicle. And in fact, this was a 60-millimetre mortar with a longer barrel. So its range was like that of an 82-millimetre weapon. And it was at Sustjepan. I know this area very well. So this was a motor vehicle that was moving about, and it would fire one, two, or three rounds, at most, and, quite simply, it would go to another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us on this map where this vehicle moved about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I can, absolutely. Cajekom is here, roughly, Sustjepan is in this area. I can't give you it exactly but it is in this general region. And it was firing at our units over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For the record, I'd like to emphasise: Are you indicating the southern side of the Dubrovacka Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Cajekom and Sustjepan. It's this area here

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself personally see that weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both the weapon and where it was firing from. I know the sound of the projectile. I recognise the sound. And it's a short distance, so you could see it very well from Golubov Kamen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just make a correction. It's not the southern side that the witness indicated, but the northern side of Rijeka Dubrovacka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not immediately able to agree. The witness indicated both sides, but firing from the southern to the northern, as I saw it indicated. Perhaps, Mr. Petrovic, you might clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also understood it the way you did, but yes, we shall clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, you said between which places did this mortar move around on the vehicle you mentioned, and what side is it of the Rijeka Dubrovacka? What area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Since I have been doing this kind of business for a long time, if this was a different scaled map I could give you the exact point, but Cajekom is right about here, Sustjepan is here, and with regard to north, south, east, west, it is the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we're clarified that point now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavicic, did you see any other hidden weapons belonging to the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, in the region I mentioned, along this road, Cajekom-Sustjepan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the term hidden. At no stage did the witness speak about a hidden weapon, but that word has been introduced by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I wasn't careful enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other weapons belonging to the Croatian side from your observation post, or rather, from your unit's positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Along here, on this part of the road, from Cajekom to Sustjepan, that communication line. And it's a hilly area. There's a place called Kamena Greda, rocky area, there are some tunnels and water. And you have a hill there. And there was a mortar on rails that they were firing from. And you can see this very well on other maps which are of a larger scale. But it's along that general communication line, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: The weapon you said was mounted on a vehicle, how did that open fire, tactically speaking, what did that weapon do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: When the first projectiles came, the vehicle was not mobile. It wasn't moving when the first projectile was fired. Now, afterwards, we had infantry coming in, and the second would fire -- there would be a second and third round. It would never fire more than two or three projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to that vehicle once it had fired those two or three projectiles?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: When these two or three projectiles were fired, the vehicle would move from Sustjepan to Gruz, and we weren't able to observe it in that area, let alone do anything about it and target it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what direction would this vehicle take?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Towards Gruz. It's this area here, from Sustjepan towards Gruz and town. Gruz is a part of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say towards town, what town do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The broader area. I lived in Dubrovnik, so that's why I can say. Towards Gruz, and Gruz is part of the town. Here it is here. This is it. So this is where Gruz starts. And it would be lost from sight there. We weren't able to see it after that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: From the position of your mortar company, what targets were you able to target? What was the ultimate range of the weapons that your company had?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: As to the technical data, the 120-millimetre mortar could reach a range of 6.200 metres, which on the map is roughly like this. It's not a very precise map, but this is Srdj here, Bosanka Srdj, and that was the longest range, the furthest distance, and it was rarely resorted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Old Town of Dubrovnik, was that within that range, within the range of your mortar company's weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. Far from it. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: In view of the tactical and technical characteristics of the mortar itself, can the mortar be positioned successfully and used from a motor vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: It can be used; however, how precise it would be is difficult to say, in view of the fact that these are new circumstances and conditions. But it can be successful, but its precision we're talking about and the technical feasibility. Mortars from vehicles can only be used if they are 60 to 82 millimetres. But mortars of a higher calibre cannot be installed without special devices. So a maximum of 82-millimetres is one that can be installed on this kind of vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how can you install an 82-millimetre mortar or 60-millimetre mortar on a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: You can do this in several ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly slow down, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best. One of the ways -- yes, it can be done. One of the ways that we use when a mortar is placed in a position where you don't have the right surface to position it on, what we do is to amortise [as interpreted] the device. We put sandbags down. That is one of the simplest and most practical ways, to use sandbags. The other method is to see that the base is welded to a surface, another surface, and then you can also use the mortar from a motor vehicle if you resort to that second option.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, in the rules for mortars, do they look into the alternative methods of using it, of installing it and positioning it? Do the handbooks on weapons of this kind provide for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the rules of regulations for an 82-millimetre mortar, this other variation is stipulated, how to place it in swampy ground, where it can be immersed, where an immersion surface is great, and on the roofs of buildings. You can also place a mortar on the roofs of buildings in the way I have just stipulated. So those are one of the variants that were provided for at that time in the manuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please: In view of the rules and regulations of the JNA, within the composition of which units during this time in 1991 was -- were the mortars? What units did they come under, these mortars, according to the establishment and its rules?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, I've been in the army a long time, and in 1988, those weapons were not within the infantry composition. It was both the infantry and artillery, depending on the unit in question. However, when the new establishment came out - and it was the last official establishment and formation in 1988 of the JNA in peacetime - within the composition of the battalion, you had 120 and 82-millimetre mortars. Otherwise, this was professionally called the mixed mortar battery. From 1988, it existed in official terms in the establishment of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "in the establishment of a battalion," what branch of the army do you mean? The land forces, or rather, the motorised battalion and infantry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During this period --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no interpretation on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The witness's response has not gone down in the transcript, Your Honour, the previous response.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Follow that up, Mr. Petrovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "battalion," tell us, please, which branch of the army you mean.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I mean the infantry, or land forces, as a branch and service of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another area now. During this period of time, that is to say, from the 19th of September, were there any more significant -- was there any significant movement of the front line, where your battalion was, the lines where your battalion was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. It was the position we took up on the 19th, and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the positions of your unit, did Admiral Jokic come by?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of November we reported to the commander, the commandeer of the unit did, and Admiral Jokic came to see us at that time, and he was present when the commander reported to him about the situation in the unit and the problems he had encountered. And after that, we received orders. We received a specific order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait a moment. Where did Admiral Jokic come?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic came, escorted by Brigade Commander Vicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please concentrate on my question. I asked you where.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: He came to the command post of the battalion's command, and it is on the map. It is the command post of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who came with Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vicic, commander of the brigade, whom I knew, came, and another group of officers. I don't know who they were. And there were some ten policemen wearing flak jackets who were escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did the meeting -- what was the meeting like, the meeting between your -- no. I withdraw that question. Who attended the meeting on your side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: On our side, the commandeers of the battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say commandeers of units, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The commanders of the companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The mortar company and the infantry company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how did the meeting evolve? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: As was customary, there was a brief report by the battalion commander, informing the admiral, Admiral Jokic, of the situation in the unit, and the problems that the unit had encountered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Admiral Jokic speak at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: When the meeting -- or rather, when the battalion commander completed his reporting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat who issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who issued assignments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Assignments were issued personally by Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What assignment was issued by Admiral Jokic, and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic issued an assignment to the battalion commander of the following content, that they should launch an attack and that part of the unit or battalion should go and take control of the Mokosica Komolac communication and road to cut off that communication line and thereby to prevent any supplies coming in to the units of the Croatian side by road, by land, which were in Dubrovnik. Cut off their supplies. And the features and facilities were stipulated. The communication line had to be cut at the hamlet of Rozat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us on the map? Can you show us what the assignment was and what area it comprised, this assignment given by Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The unit was supposed to go down from Golubov Kamen to the region of Rozata, down this serpentine road, this is a large area and slope but we had to reach Rozat. It's not very visible on the map. But we had to cut across the communication line here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Show us once again what the position was?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not clear as to what time frame this testimony refers to. Perhaps a clarification would assist the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll leave that to Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time period you are referring to? What was the time period when Admiral Jokic visited and the order issued by him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of November, or, more specifically, I think it was probably on the 8th or 9th of November, thereabouts. I'm not quite sure of the date, but the 8th or the 9th of November, 1991. That's when the meeting was held and the following day we set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us where your battalion's positions were at that point in time and what axes of attack had Admiral Jokic ordered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The position of the battalion, which is recorded on the map, was as it is here, Golubov Kamen was the axis, and the shortest route down to Rozat. And as I say, the shortest route on the map wouldn't be possible, but there's a place called Obuljeno, between Mokosica and Rozat, so we had to go from Golubov Kamen, Obuljeno, Rozata. That was the axis of attack and that was the line we were supposed to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Also, could you show us on the map what the target of the attack was, the attack ordered by Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The objective was that the forces in Dubrovnik, Croatian forces in Komolac and Dubrovnik on this side of Rijeka Dubrovacka, so to cut off the communication and thereby prevent the supply along the land routes to the units in Dubrovnik. That was the main task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was specifically the assignment of your mortar company in this attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: As part of this attack, my unit was supposed to offer fire support for the implementation of this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were the firing targets determined, or the targets that your unit was supposed to fire on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is always done. The preparation for firing elements is always carried out, so we did have several targets. We specifically knew what the attack -- the target of attack was supposed to be, so we were -- we did prepare for firing at those targets. We prepared for fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long Admiral Jokic stayed in your command that day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: He spent about an hour or an hour and a half at the command. He came at about 9.30 and left the command post at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the attack start, the one that he had ordered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The next day, at 4.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this the first action that was supposed to result in moving your line of deployment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did the action proceed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander in the early morning hours of the next day changed the axis of attack a little bit, so he tried to do it in the shortest possible way, Golubov Kamen, Rozat, to come to the communication, under cover of the night, without action by the mortars, which we succeeded in, for the most part. During the morning, since this is very difficult terrain, our units clashed for the first time with the Croat forces at Rozat where they were surrounded. Then, at the request of the unit commander to open fire and to help the units to pull out, we opened fire in the Rozat sector, specifically at Rozat, the Rozat cemetery, and we managed to pull out the unit. Or to put it in a different way, the attack did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did your unit sustain any casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first operation, and we did have the first casualties in our battalion. One soldier was killed and four or five soldiers were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown -- could the witness please be shown Exhibit D57.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document and tell us, first of all, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: This is an order for attack. It's one of the documents issued by the commander for the implementation of any task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which command issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 4 -- actually, paragraph 4, on page 2 of the B/C/S version of the document. Could you please read that and tell us what kind of action is discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: This is a decision. It's the fourth order -- the fourth paragraph of the command, by introducing the 3/5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it to yourself and then tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. It is specified here what needs to be done. So from here I can only see which our part of that is. And it says specifically here to break out at the Komolac-Rijeka-Dubravacka line and establish full blockade of Dubrovnik, and a blockade could not be established for as long as the communication is not severed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 5, 5.1 and 5.2, but primarily 5.1. What are the tasks that are being discussed there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the axis that I mentioned a little while ago: Carry out the attack along Pobrezje, Mokosica, Obuljeno, Rozat, and unite with the forces of the 3rd Battalion. That is what is of interest for us. That was the target that we were supposed to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this document constitute a written order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: If it's signed, it was certified, so this is an absolutely valid document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is the order being issued -- in this order, the action that we discussed being ordered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the parts of it that refer to me. Mokosica, Obuljeno, Rozat that was the ultimate objective and target. We were not alone in participating in this action, but there was a broader operation. But basically this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The 9th of November, at 2300 hours, at 11:00 p.m. And it's the 9th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I propose that we take our first morning break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. There will be a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavicic, would you please kindly tell us about this document, D57, that you have before you. What is usually according to the rules contained in an order to attack, in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: These would be -- this would be data about the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A commander issuing an attack to order, how would he obtain the information? Based on what does he compile paragraph 1 of an order for attack?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The commanders, if we go down from the bottom to the top, from the lower levels of command, would forward these -- this information to their superiors, at the higher levels, at the brigade levels, and several units, they have their units within the brigades which are entrusted with gathering data on the enemy. There are organs that deal with these assignments, and the battalion would then receive the information from his superior commander. The commander of a company would receive the information from the commander of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose of the information under paragraph 1 in an order for attack? Why is this written?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: This is written in order to say which enemy forces are facing the unit that is about to embark on an attack, to see what they will be facing, what are their weapon strengths, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, let's look at this order for attack of the 9th of November, 1991, issued by Vice Admiral Miodrag Jokic. In item 1, amongst other things, it says: From the fortresses of the old city fortresses to attack with mortars of 60 and 82 millimetres. Why was this written?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: This is there to state that these are points where danger is coming from and which can be fired upon. It's a legitimate military target. These are firing points in order to implement the firing task. That's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please look at Exhibit D58.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document and then I will put some questions to you. Mr. Pavicic, could you please look at item 2 first of this document, whether, in a regular combat report of the 10th of November, 1991, is there a report on the activities which we saw from document D57 a little while ago and which were ordered at 2300 hours the day before, on the 9th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: From what I can see here and what refers to the unit that we were in, it states one enforced platoon of the 1st Company of the 472nd Motorised Brigade has infiltrated itself from its hitherto position in the region of Komolac. This is enough, when one is writing a report. There is no need for additional detail. So it's right here, under the first item under paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This regular combat report from the 10th of November, 1991, does it contain the report of the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector about the action ordered by Admiral Jokic at the command post and which is something that we discussed earlier during this examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: That's this part. This part refers to it. As I said, I see that this part refers to that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That is the first item in paragraph 2. Could you please look at paragraph 4. Does that contain a report of the casualties during that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I looked at this item, and as far as I recall now, this soldier here is not here. I think this soldier did not die right away. He was heavily, serious wounded, and then he died the next day. So he could not be included in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us, as part of the military doctrine and the manner of communication amongst the commands in a regular combat report, what is the purpose of this part contained under 1?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: When any report is sent, including information about the enemy, the point is to acquaint the command with the information acquired by a lower unit, and then the Superior Command, based on all of their information, all the information coming from lower units, because each unit has a command where all the information is gathered, then all of this information is synthesised and then distributed to the commander of the units to whom this would be interesting. This is information about the enemy gathered possibly by a lower unit, and the point of it is to acquaint other units with that. As I said, there are different ways of gathering information, and the essence --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the seventh line of paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has not finished his response. He's been cut off midway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that was a reasonable interruption. Carry on, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 1, that has to do with the enemy, and it's line 7 where it says: The hotel, the ramparts. And it says: With MB. Does that mean that the command of the 9th VPS informs its superior commands about enemy activity, as it says there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pavicic: Until when was your unit at this position that we saw on the map on document P124?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: My unit was there until the end of November, or rather, the 28th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Where was your unit located after that, and how did the relocation of your unit take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: During the night of the 28th of November, we received orders to march and to deploy the unit in the area of the village of Podimoc. It's about 50 kilometres from this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document P132, which is a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could this map please be zoomed in. Mr. Pavicic, could you please adjust the map so that we can see where the new position of your unit was after the 28th. Can you show us where this is, and can you tell us what area this is, close to which bigger village or town.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: This is the 1st Motorised Battalion. It's right over here. This is where my mortar unit is. I can see now -- yes. As I said, the village of Podimoc. That's where the command was, and it's marked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's a bigger place in the vicinity, so that we can orient ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, all of these are very small villages. So it's Visocani maybe. That's perhaps the biggest place in the entire area. That's a bit further ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please: Where was your unit taken at the end of November? Within what group was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The entire brigade was then transferred into the 2nd Corps, and that included my battalion too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions from me. Mr. Pavicic, tell us, please: Do you know whether the other side used places of worship for opening fire against your units in this period that we are discussing, October, November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: As for what I saw myself, during the action that I described previously, that is to say, at Rozat, there is a cemetery in the village of Rozat and a church, or rather, a monastery, from which fire was opened at our units. Specifically, they were opening mortar fire from graves, and they were also firing with recoilless guns of 82 millimetres from the church. I saw that myself, and this caused major problems for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that this is -- or rather, this is a monastery, isn't it? So is a monastery a cultural and historical monument?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. That's not a question this witness could respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any abuses of places like churches and monasteries by the Croatian side and that you know about it in this period that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, and that is what I learned in school, like anywhere else in the world, that is what we are taught. And they fired from monasteries. And, say, firing from a grave, I think that's absurd. And then also opening gunfire from a church or monastery. Because if fire is opened, then the place where fire is opened from is a legitimate military objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the unit that you were in? Was it made aware of the rules of the international law of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. You see, whenever an officer begins his studies at the military academy, one of the first things that is taught is law, international law of war and the rules that have to be observed. So every officer, every trained officer, has to know very well what he's allowed to do and what he's not allowed to do. I, as an officer, knew about these things. And after all, you don't even need to resort to the law; just do not do unto others what you don't want done to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the members of your unit? Did you make them aware of this, that is, the rules of international law of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. And all levels of command, at the level of battalion, brigade, et cetera, either through orders, directives, instructions. We received specific instructions. And even within each and every order, the rights and responsibilities of units are spelled out specifically, like the treatment of prisoners and various other elements that are not directly related to combat. So this is spelled out precisely in the order concerned, and then we would make the unit members aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavicic. Now you are going to be answering the questions of my learned friends. And this concludes the examination-in-chief that I had, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pavicic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You testified that you're currently the deputy commander of the school for non-commissioned officers. Do you hold a rank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I do have a rank, and it is not a school for non-commissioned officers. There's a big difference involved. It's a school of reserve officers. And yes, I do hold a rank. The rank is lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that misunderstanding, but that's how it was recorded in the transcript. And since you're a lieutenant colonel, I'll refer to you as colonel. Colonel, when did you join the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was that transfer that was made, where you came from your school to the 472nd Motorised Brigade, did the intent of -- were you informed that you were being deployed to participate in the Dubrovnik operation? Were you aware of that at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. I did not know that. I received through regular channels an order to report to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. To a particular -- to a particular form of wording that is used yesterday -- that was used yesterday and that is used today. The witness before you never said the Dubrovnik operation, never used that word. So I think that it is improper to make that kind of assertion. Not at a given -- not a at any given time, either yesterday or today, the previous witness or Mr. Pavicic, they never used those words, "the Dubrovnik operation." Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are shades of description. Dubrovnik was the focus of attention of the first witness's evidence. But your point is made, Mr. Petrovic. Carry on, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will avoid using the word "operation," perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Going back, Colonel: Where did you report to when you were transferred to the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: According to the rules, to the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question is where, to what location? Was it to the command post; and if so, where was the command post of the 472nd Motorised Brigade located at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: At that time, the command post was in Trebinje, in the town of Trebinje, in the barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you testified in examination-in-chief that the original unit to which the brigade belonged was the 9th Naval Sector. And when you used the term "original unit," did you mean that during peacetime, the 472nd Motorised Brigade was within the composition of the 9th Naval Sector? Is that what you intended to say or is it correct to say it in that manner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was within that composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in late September, the 472nd Motorised Brigade was taken out of the 9th Naval Sector and subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group command; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And thereafter, the 9th Naval Sector was separately --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It's a little difficult the way I am ...
