utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And thereafter, the 9th Naval Sector was directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group, separately from the 472nd Motorised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it's a difficult question. At the time when I was commander, I didn't really see the entire picture. You have to know what re-subordination is, and also what unit reinforcement means. These are two interesting military terms, and people who are unfamiliar with them can have a problem. It is true that it --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. May I make this much clearer. If the witness may be shown Defence Exhibit document D44. Colonel, I'm going to show you a document which has been tendered into evidence by the Defence on behalf of General Strugar. And while that is -- the document is being retrieved, would you please examine the document and tell me whether the document reflects that at that stage, the 9th VPS, separately from the 472nd Motorised Brigade, and the 472nd Motorised Brigade quite outside the 9th VPS are directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group, and the 2nd Operational Group is issuing orders or specifying assignments which should be tasks to these two units, among other units, in the course of an operation. Does this document reflect that to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: You see, this is actually a proposed decision. A decision is not the same type of document as an order is. You should bear that in mind. A proposal is a proposal. The superior can take it into account or can dismiss it. I cannot tell you exactly, but on the basis of what is written here, it can be seen that the 472nd Motorised Brigade was under the command of the 2nd Operational Group, but I would not like to go into details, because at that time it was a very sensitive issue, as far as I'm concerned. Now I am familiar with the subject matter involved, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Does this proposal also indicate that the 9th VPS is also at that time directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group? Can you see that from this document? It is indicated so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is a proposal being issued by the command of the 2nd Operational Group to the General Staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the course of the operation in and around Dubrovnik, the 472nd Motorised Brigade was re-subordinated to the 9th VPS, specifically, on the 25th of October; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: However, even at that stage, the 9th VPS was still directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a bit hard to say, but that's the way it turns out. Or rather, not the way it turns out; that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you another document, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown D43.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is also a document which has been tendered into evidence by the Defence. Could you please examine this document, and doesn't this document reflect the fact that on 25th October 1991, the 2nd Operational Group takes the decision to subordinate the 472nd Motorised Brigade to the 9th VPS? The document is signed by the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you properly, you said subordinated, or re-subordinated, if I understood you correctly. Is that what you said? It says here that it is being returned to its original unit, so we're not talking about re-subordination. It was sent elsewhere, and now it is returning to its original unit. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point is not the word, the term I used. My point is that at that stage, still, the 9th VPS is subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group. That's my point. You agree with me? If you are uncomfortable with using the word "subordination," let us say the 9th VPS was within the composition of the 2nd Operational Group at that stage, when 472nd Motorised Brigade is being returned to the 9th VPS. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, I agree only partly, because I did not focus on this word by accident, because it has to do with command. That is very important. If you go back to your original unit, your original house, so to speak, you know who the head of the household is, who the commander is. What you asked me is very important. Re-subordination and subordination is one thing, whereas returning is a different matter. So there is no further comment that I need to make. This is a very specific document that refers to it unequivocally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question. Are you aware that in the course of the operations conducted in and around Dubrovnik, the 9th VPS was within the command of the 2nd Operational Group, in that the 2nd Operational Group command controlled and commanded the 9th VPS activities? And to make it easier for you to respond to this, let me show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown D47. This is also a document tendered into evidence by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, do you see that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, that this document, which is dated 18 November 1991, has been issued -- this is an order issued by the command of the 2nd Operational Group to the command of the 9th VPS, and it's signed by General Strugar. And by this order, General Strugar is issuing orders to the 9th VPS command, giving it specific tasks as to how to carry out naval activity around Dubrovnik? Do you agree with me? Isn't it the case? Isn't it clear from this document that General Strugar is issuing orders to the 9th VPS command with regard to naval tasks, and this is a document tendered into evidence by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. But look, I don't agree that this is a type of order, an order for attack or whatever you called it. We know how orders are written. This is not the way orders are written. This is issuing assignments and guidelines. On the basis of this, the commander of the 9th VPS will --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I interrupt. This is a document tendered into evidence by the Defence, not by the Prosecution. So unless you are suggesting that the Defence would be tendering documents which are not correct. I mean, this is a document that has been tendered into evidence by the Defence. And I'm putting to you that this document reflects clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I intervene at this point. The witness didn't challenge anything with respect to the document. He's explaining the document, and he was interrupted in his explanations of the document. He wasn't allowed to finish his explanation and to tell us the difference between this document and an order. That's what he wanted to explain, but he wasn't allowed to do so. Otherwise, he doesn't express any doubts as to the authenticity of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I entirely agree, Mr. Petrovic. I would have thought that you had well and truly got the answers you want, Ms. Mahindaratne, and that you could very quickly move on to something --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Since you were in --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the document be returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Since you were in Dubrovnik and deployed in and around Dubrovnik, are you familiar -- were you involved in any way with the operations conducted by the JNA forces, the 2nd Operational Group forces, in October 1991? And I'm referring specifically to the operations carried out on the 23rd, 24th, and 25th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I've already said that my unit did not move, so not the battalion and especially not firing by mortars from these positions. The first firing took place at the beginning of November. So we didn't move at all. So I consider that we were in our place, at our positions, deployed on this part of the terrain. We didn't move.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was: Do you know that operations were conducted by the 2nd Operational Group forces on the 23rd, 24th, and 25th October? That was my question, not as to whether your unit participated.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I wasn't in a position to see what the other units were doing and conducting, so I can't say. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question is: Do you know, not whether you saw, do you know whether the 2nd Operational Group forces conducted an operation during this period? That's all I want to know. Do you know? Not whether you saw anything or any other aspect of it, but just do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I don't really understand your question. Because where I was, myself, first of all, I couldn't see anything; and as a soldier and officer looking at the broader area, I do know what the tasks of the superior units to me and Superior Command to me was. But all this was within the frameworks of the deblockade of the town of Dubrovnik. So I am aware of that, but I don't know anything further than that. I don't know any of the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your unit was returned or directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group around 21st November 1991. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not the case. It is not what the witness said. It is quite simply not the testimony of this witness. He said, and we could check this out, I don't want to suggest what, but quite simply the witness did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm putting a question to the witness. It was a suggestion. The witness could respond to it either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had hoped that we had finished all together with subordination and returning of units and so on. Surely that area has been well covered and that you're going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I was on the point of in November. This was much later. I was earlier on dealing with October subordination. But if Your Honour so wishes, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And before you do, could I ask the witness: Is it your evidence that you heard no concerted firing and no artillery or mortar fire in the period 23rd, 24th, 25th of October, from where you were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the firing. There was firing. I don't challenge that. But I don't know the details of the firing. I know that it was within the broader operation of the deblockade of Dubrovnik, and my level of command couldn't have known about that or couldn't have been aware of that. I know about it now, as lieutenant colonel, but I was a captain at that time and didn't have any insight into the operational group and brigade's activities. So there was fighting, but what the object and target of the fighting was, I can't say, the facilities, the targets, and so on. But that you could hear firing, yes, you could. But what was actually happening, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm sorry, Ms. Mahindaratne. You were asking about operations at the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll get to that later on, Your Honour. I will move on with a different line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, wasn't the 472nd Motorised Brigade a very strong brigade in terms of personnel and weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, that was certainly an elite unit of the former JNA, both in terms of manpower and in terms of equipment and materiel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And it had approximately 6.000 personnel attached to it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. When everything was mobilised and when you have a 100 per cent mobilisation. In this specific case, I would say the figure was somewhat lower.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the brigade had four battalions, including your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During peacetime, the brigade had only one battalion and three companies, and isn't it the case that during wartime, these three companies are built up into battalion levels, by mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: That's what I said at the beginning. And this is how it was, roughly. It's true that that battalion in peacetime had three companies, filled with regular soldiers. But our battalion and the others, up to company level, four motorised ones, so there were other units too, they were replenished with the reserve force on the basis of mobilisation. So the live battalion - and I use this term in inverted commas, live - that wasn't replenished. It was just brought up to a full complement if the need arose. It was always ready for deployment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And each of the battalions had four companies which had 82-millimetre mortars, Maljutkas, rocket artillery, tanks, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but a battalion does not have any tanks, and you're talking about rocket artillery. I don't know about that. The strongest weapon that a battalion possesses is a 120-millimetre mortar, by virtue of firepower and calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was going to get to that. Each of those battalions had 120-millimetre mortar support battery?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Now, whether they were all mobilised, I don't know about that for the other battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, going back to November, I asked you a question which was that the 472nd Motorised Brigade was re-subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group on 21st November, at which point my learned friend interrupted. Is that correct or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but would you repeat that. What did you say? The 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On 21st of November, the 472nd Motorised Brigade, including your unit, was re-subordinated or brought within the command of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That wasn't in November. It moved to the 2nd Corps. That was later on, in actual fact, the 2nd Corps, not the operational group any more. It was the 2nd Corps later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the 2nd Corps was within the command of the 2nd Operational Group, wasn't it? You do know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure about such matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where was your unit deployed in early November?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: In early November, where we were on the 19th --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... as a date, I will give you 5th November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The 5th of November, the same place it was on the 19th of September, that is, around the region of the village of Zaplanik. That was the basic firepower position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you know that at that stage, on 5th November, there was a move, or there was an order, which was of course not carried out, for your unit and the other units of the 472nd Motorised Brigade to withdraw from those positions. And to assist you with your response, may the witness be shown Exhibit P125, tab 23. Tab 23 of Jokic Prosecution binder. I appreciate that you may not have seen this document before, but would you please examine this order. And does it indicate to you that at this stage, certain units have arrived at your positions on the basis that the 472nd Motorised Brigade units were to withdraw from certain -- or to be relieved from duty and withdraw from those positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: From this order, I can see that we were supposed to withdraw on the 6th and to be replaced by the Territorial Defence detachment of Trebinje. Now, why that wasn't done, I really don't know. But judging by this document, I can see that that was supposed to have happened with respect to the 1st Battalion. I don't know. I'm looking at this now. Now, why it wasn't implemented, I really don't know. If that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Of course it does. And when did you -- did your unit and the other units of the 472nd Motorised Brigade actually withdraw from those positions? Would you repeat the date if you have already said it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of November, the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And up until the time you withdrew, your unit withdrew from -- on 28th November, did you -- did the unit retain the weapons which the unit had earlier on? Were the weapons in place at those particular positions right through that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you probably mean the artillery pieces. Weapons are one thing; artillery pieces are another, and mortars in particular. If that's what you mean, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to mortars, artillery, Maljutkas.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I use military terminology. For me, artillery is a level higher up. There are Howitzers, rocket units and so on. But mortars are within the battalion composition, and that was retained, from day one to the last day. We left it as we arrived. So nothing was added or taken away. As to the other artillery pieces, I don't know. That would be a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You testified in examination-in-chief that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The document can be returned. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- that the transfer of your unit -- I'm sorry. Your transfer to the 472nd Motorised Brigade on 15th September 1991 was pursuant to an order issued by the command of the 9th Naval Sector, or command of the naval sector. That's what you said in evidence in chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order of the navy commander, and it was under his competence to send officers from one unit to another. Specifically, where we were, that was pursuant to an order from him. And then all the orders down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you have that order with you, or in a position to produce it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, had I known, I would have taken it with me, but I can send it to you. I haven't got it here, no. I didn't take it to The Hague. But of course I would be willing to send you the document at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your commander of the 472nd Motorised Brigade is Obrad -- or was Obrad Vicic; is that correct? Obrad Vicic. I'm sorry for the mispronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of certain combat activity conducted by the Croat forces from positions such as Strincijera, Bosanka, so on and so forth. All those positions, that is, Strincijera, Bosanka, and the locations in that area were captured by the 2nd Operational Group forces in the course of the November operations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No, not quite so. Because these points are closer to Srdj, so not everything was taken. There was some kind of line in between in the beginning. So not all of the points or the elevations were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What were the elevations taken in November? Strincijera was taken in November, isn't it? I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Well, I don't know exactly. From my position, the deployment of the units, other different units attacked along those axes. So I don't know exactly to show you on the map where that line went, by 100 or 200 metres, but I think that all the features that you mentioned were not captured. I know that terrain, so it's very difficult to see that on the ground from the position where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you a map bearing P132. It was shown to you earlier on. Could you please -- Colonel, could you please place your pointer on that area where you have indication of the positions of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to ask that the witness first be shown the entire map so that he can see the time period that this refers to. The map is now folded so he cannot see exactly which time period is covers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please place your pointer on those positions held by the 3rd Battalion, the companies, yes, the three companies.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Zarkovica was captured in October; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Zarkovica is on the other side. I wasn't able to see that, so I don't know exactly when this was captured. This is something that you could not see from our positions, in view of the configuration of the terrain, you could not see that from Srdj, from Bosanka, from the hill. It's not possible to see that part. All I could see was Rijeka Dubrovacka and the northern slopes and this is as we had it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just yes or no answer would do. Do you know that Zarkovica was captured in October --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that those three positions indicated there, where the 3rd Battalion companies are, that is, Bosanka and the other two positions, that they were captured in the course of the November operation? Do you know or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you know that the 3rd Battalion participated in the November operations, the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that it took part in the operations, but I'm not aware of the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the Old Town was shelled in the course of the November operation. Surely you would know that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Even up to today, you don't know that the Old Town was shelled in the course of the November operation. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Up until today, I don't know that officially. All I heard about is that there was shelling on the 6th of December, but beyond that, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said up until today you don't know that officially. Did you find out unofficially? Did you hear about it, either through media or colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I heard that there was shelling, but on the 6th of December, and I don't know about it in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What orders had you received from your higher command with regard to the Old Town, as to what you could or could not do in engaging -- in the course of combat with regard to the Old Town? Did you receive any specific orders saying: Do not fire on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the superior officer, from the very beginning of the operations, practically from October 1st onwards, it was explicitly ordered that no one should dare to fire on the Old Town. But this was mostly part of the measures. I said that this was what was written in the order. But in view of the characteristics of our weapons and the distance we were at, it was not possible to do it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you were shown two documents in the course of examination-in-chief, D57 and D58.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown those two documents again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, D57 is dated 9th November and has been issued at 23 hours, which means that those tasks that have been issued were with regard to assignments to be carried out the next day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And D58, as questioned by the learned Defence counsel, is the combat report based on those activities carried out the next day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And D58 is a report sent to the command of the 2nd Operational Group by the 9th VPS. It's a combat report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is the type of combat reports a unit would send up to its higher command in reporting on what combat activity they had taken and reporting the ground situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that in D58 there's a reference to a soldier who had not been killed, but it includes -- his name is included in the list of those killed. But you are personally aware that he was not killed at this stage, that he was only wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Look, on the 10th, in the morning -- well, this is not so important, in view of the documentation. There is a list of people who were killed in that operation. One, that soldier was wounded. A bullet went through his head, his skull. He was in a coma. I don't know whether there was surgery or something, but he didn't die that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point is: You said that this document -- that the soldier's name, which has been put down as one of those killed, is incorrect. I mean, is it a yes or no? You said that this soldier was not killed at this stage, and that's what you're saying right now too.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The soldier was not killed, but he is not on this list. He could not have been. This is a report for that day. That soldier died the following day, so he could not be on this list for this day. I explained that. His name is not on this list. He was seriously wounded and he died the following day. So he could not be on this list. This is a list of the 10th, from the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what you're saying, then, is that this report contains factually incorrect information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood the original evidence --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- Ms. Mahindaratne. The witness did not suggest the name was on the list. Not in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I probably misunderstood what he said. I was under the impression that he said there is a name here -- okay. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, could I just follow it up for a moment and then we might be able to move on. You named a soldier who was wounded on the 9th and you think died perhaps on the 10th whose name is not on that list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The soldier was not wounded on the 9th but on the 10th, in the morning. We went out for our operation on the 10th. So he died on the 11th. And that is why he could not be on this list. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, instead of clearing things up, I've made them less clear, because I understood from your evidence that Admiral Jokic visited on the 8th and you commenced operations on the 9th, and that this report of the 10th was a report on the first day's operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I didn't know the exact day when the admiral came to see us. I don't know if it was the 8th or the 9th. I cannot recall that. But in any case, the following day, after his visit, we set out on our attack. We had that one seriously wounded person, who actually died 24 hours after being wounded. According to this report, I see where people are from. That soldier was an active-duty soldier, so he was not on this list. He could not have been included on this list. I'm sorry that I don't know the first and last name of that soldier, because then it would be easier to compare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. I was going to ask you whether that report mentioned both killed and wounded. It does, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does here, yes, both of the killed and the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the soldier you knew to be wounded is not shown on the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is only one soldier here mentioned as being wounded, soldier Jovo Kodalovic [phoen], as being seriously wounded, municipality of Kotor. This is confusing me a little bit. I cannot remember. He was an active-duty soldier. I'm not sure whether the place of origin was written down in the case of active-duty soldiers. It's possible. I'm not ruling it out. It's possible. But I am sorry that I don't have the name so that we could resolve this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think I've helped anybody, Ms. Mahindaratne, so please carry on as you were going to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know about the activities of the other units attached to the 472nd Motorised Brigade, but do you know of any colleagues attached to the other units and not your units who were killed or injured, wounded in combat operations? And I'm referring to the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: It's a broad question. I'm not quite clear on this question. What are we talking about? What time period?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For example, in the November operations, do you know of any soldiers belonging to the other units of the 472nd Motorised Brigade who were killed or injured in the course of the November operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases in other units. There was talk about people who were killed and wounded. I don't know the names, but I did hear that this was talked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know of such soldiers belonging to the other units killed or wounded in the course of the operations conducted on 23rd, 24th, and 25th of October?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates of who was killed, when. But if we're talking about the fighters, whether they were killed or wounded, this was something that was talked about, but I don't know who was killed, when, where. This is a very large subject. I didn't know from which units they were. I don't know where they were killed and who they were, but there were people who were killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was not as to the details of those who were wounded and killed, but whether you were aware of those who were killed and wounded in the October operations. And do I take your response as a yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I had the impression that you asked about November a little while ago, and now you're talking about October. So excuse me, but I didn't hear that. I thought you were speaking about November. But now you're speaking about October. I apologise if I misheard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to October. I'm asking you -- it's a simple question. Do you know of any other soldiers belonging to other units of the 472nd Motorised Brigade killed or wounded in the course of the combat operations conducted on 23rd, 24th, and 25th October? Yes or no. Do you know of soldiers who belonged -- it's a simple question, Mr. -- Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were wounded and killed in other units in that period. I don't know the details. But there were such cases, both killed and wounded, in that time period that you are talking about, in October.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So which would then definitely indicate to you that there were combat operations going on during this period. Isn't that the case? Isn't it a clear inference, if you knew that soldiers belonging to other units were killed in combat during this period, that there had to be combat operations then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: You must know that there were a lot of casualties during the various truces or during the time the units were on positions, as a result of fire from the Croatian side. So I'm not sure. I don't know that there were combat operations, but we still had casualties. I know about units which were also in positions similar to my units who had suffered casualties but were not in the process of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on. You testified about Admiral Jokic visiting prior to the November operations and giving certain instructions, and you just stated that you were not certain as to the exact date. Do you remember where Admiral Jokic came to? What was the location?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: He came in the beginning of November. I do not know the exact date, whether it was the 8th or the 9th. I'm not sure about the actual date. To the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion and you have this marked on the map. This command post is between Zaplanik and Hum halfway. It's called the speleological house and that's where the command post was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you stated further that the battalion commander reported to Admiral Jokic about certain issues. Who was the battalion commander? Is the battalion commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what is his name?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name. The interpreters could not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, you are being asked to repeat the name. The interpreters did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Major Milivoje Kadovic. At that time he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another area. You spoke of seeing a 60-millimetre mortar. You said a 60-millimetre long-barrelled artillery piece which was similar to an 82-millimetre mortar mounted on a vehicle firing from a certain areas, and those areas that you described are the wider area of Dubrovnik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Specifically, between Cajkovici and Sustjepan. That's where I noticed firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where were you when you saw this vehicle? From where did you observe this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: From Golubov Kamen, the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is the distance between this observation post to those areas, that is -- I'm sorry, I'm going to mispronounce. Sustjepan and -- and the other place that you indicated. What is the distance between these two places?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Between Sustjepan and Cajkovici? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Or from where I was observing?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: From where you were observing.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Oh, between Sustjepan and the observation post, there are a few kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many kilometres? Could you just indicate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Less than two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That would be -- if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown map P124.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please place your pointer on the location that you were, the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is that the place you indicated, Golubov Kamen, your observation post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And would you please indicate where the vehicle was when you observed it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The vehicle was almost halfway between Sustjepan and Cajkovici. It's approximately this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how did you observe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How did you observe it? Did you observe it with your naked eye? Were you watching this? Were you involved in combat activity at the time you saw this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. I was at the observation post, and I was observing. First I saw the projectile, with the naked eye. I saw activity and then I identified it through binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You went on to say that a mortar could be used from a vehicle subject to the vehicle being prepared in a special way. Now, isn't it the case that when a mortar is fired, there is a recoil, which has to be absorbed by a soft substance or soft surface? Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And so even if you do position sandbags on a vehicle, still, wouldn't the recoil damage the surface of the truck or the surface on which the weapon is placed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: For 60-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars, that cannot happen. If the surface is prepared properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Don't you have to add additional suspension to the vehicle and reinforce the strength of the vehicle in order to carry out firing of mortars from a vehicle? Otherwise the vehicle would be completely destroyed after a few firings from the mortar, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the part where the surface is going to be has to be reinforced. Metal can be placed down there, whatever, and then the suspension or the sandbags have to be put there by way of reinforcement. I could not see from such a distance. And for these small-calibre mortars of 60 millimetres or 82 millimetres, that is what is done. It does not fire a maximum number of charges, so there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So how many times can you fire from a vehicle in a given situation? Can it fire more than a couple of times, at the most?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, if the surface was prepared properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What type of a truck or vehicle can you use for this type of activity? Doesn't it -- shouldn't it be a huge vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. No. Even the smallest possible freight vehicle, from one and a half tonnes onwards. It doesn't really matter. From one and a half tonnes onwards. What really matters is the chassis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you said that there was firing from this truck and you observed this, was it clear to you that it was being used as a means of provocation? And I'm referring to the time you observed the firing from the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, that was already activity against our units, because the projectiles were falling right behind me, 100 or 200 metres behind me. So the objective was to fire at the front line of the battalion units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a good time to take a break? And thereafter I will not take more than 15 minutes, 10 minutes, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it practical for you to conclude in the next 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may, if it's after the break, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You need to collect your thoughts?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break now, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have only one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Colonel, in the course of examination-in-chief, you referred to certain problems caused to the 472nd Motorised Brigade due to the former commander, Colonel Marinovic, leaving, and also due to the senior officers not knowing each other, et cetera. Now, did these problems also have an impact on the level of discipline of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when the commander left the unit, this did have a negative effect on the unit as a whole. However, part of the officers remained, part of the permanent officers. And this pertains primarily to the new units that were mobilised, where the soldiers and officers came from elsewhere. They had more problems. As for discipline, the problem that you asked about, I can just say, for my own unit and, to a large extent, the battalion, we did not have any problems in that respect, not major problems. We had some minor problems perhaps. But 70 per cent of the officers came from Bileca, from the reserve officers school. These were primarily officers who were very good, who were excellent. So we established a system. We knew what the rules and regulations were, so we did not have any problems in that respect. Specifically, I did not have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your unit in particular, but did you observe certain problems relating to discipline perhaps amongst those units that were newly mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, these were sporadic problems that I could see at a given point in time. I heard that there were some very small problems, but I cannot talk about any major problems. I was not there. I was dealing with the mobilisation of my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have just one more question, Your Honour. I'm sorry, it wasn't the last question, after all. How long have you served in the VRS, Colonel? If you can indicate from when to when.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: From 1993 until the present day. I'm still in service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you just identify what VRS stands for. I mean, it's army of what? For the record.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska. That's the abbreviation, the acronym.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have concluded cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pavicic, my colleague asked you a few minutes ago about discipline. Tell us, please: What was the fire discipline like in your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: In my case, we only opened fire on the orders issued by the battalion commander, only on his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases of arbitrary firing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. That could not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, in response to the question put by my learned friend, you described the 472nd Brigade as an elite unit in the former JNA in peacetime. Given all the problems that the unit had in this period - September, October, November - can that unit still be called an elite unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: I think that in that period, it was, to a considerable degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: In this period - September, October, November - were there any problems in terms of manning the unit, getting certain specialties, a certain profile of soldiers, non-commissioned officers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems. For example, for some critical specialties, or very important VESs, there were problems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's questions, you talked about the establishment structure of the battalion. My colleague asked you about what was there in terms of artillery, tanks, and so on, within your motorised battalion. Tell us, please, the formation structure of the motorised battalion, does it not imply that there has to be a mortar of a certain calibre in each and every unit? Could you please explain the establishment to us. What is envisaged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion has its own command, two or three companies. A mortar company, an anti-aircraft company, and a logistics platoon. Those are the basic elements of the establishment. On the basis of these elements, certain elements of combat deployment and combat order are set up, specifically, 120-millimetre mortars set up a battalion group, which has the task of providing fire support in terms of carrying out tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Can a motorised battalion or an infantry battalion which was sent to carry out a particular task, can it leave behind, for example, a mortar company, a 120-millimetre mortar company, is something like that possible, according to doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: No. That is not possible. Absolutely. It would be as if -- if you simply left behind the quartermasters and you did not provide any food to the troops. That's what that would be like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if a battalion is deployed to a particular position, all elements of the battalion are deployed within that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. And after all, that is the basic principle of how one deploys a battalion in defence with all the elements of a combat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My colleague asked you about losses, that either your unit had or other units of the brigade that we are discussing. Do you know of any losses at Ivanjica, when the operations only started? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since in fact this was in front, if we are looking at the geography involved, I think that it was on the 3rd of October that four, five, or six men got killed, and the same number got wounded. I know some colleagues who were wounded there or killed there. So I am aware of that. I think there were five or six dead and the same number of wounded persons. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything of the circumstances of these casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of the dead persons were killed by mortar fire, three or four soldiers were, and later on in this sporadic gunfire, the provocations. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be given document D43. Perhaps it's even there right now, because my colleague asked the witness about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this document now and tell us: On the basis of this document, what can you conclude? What was the original unit of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: We can see that the original unit was the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean when we say "original unit"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: It means that it is part of the 9th Military Naval Sector. In the chain of command, the 9th Military Naval Sector is responsible and under the chain of command for that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, when the brigade is given over to the 2nd Corps, is this only temporary, provisional, before the unit withdraws from its original unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: It depends on the type of assignment. It can be for a longer period of time or a smaller period. Re-subordination is one thing, temporary composition is another, and restructuring is another thing yet again. In this case, it returned to its original unit, Maticnje [phoen]. And when we come to the 2nd Operational Group, before that, it was within the composition of the 2nd group for a particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, at the beginning, remained within the composition of the 9th VPS, Naval Military Sector?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PAVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. I did not raise any issues about the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's true, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions in redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. May we thank you, Mr. Pavicic, for your evidence and assistance here, and you'll be pleased to know you're now free to return to your home and work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Rodic, will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence calls the next witness, who is Gojko Djurasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djurasic. Would you be kind enough to take the card from the court officer and read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, would you introduce yourself, please, to the Trial Chamber by giving them your full name.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: My name is Gojko Djurasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you give us your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: The 17th of August, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where you reside.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I reside in Bar, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what your profession is.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I'm a pensioner at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what education you have.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Primary school, secondary school; after that, I went to the military academy anti-aircraft attack section in Zadar, and the General Staff Academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means you were an active-duty officer?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And your military career in the Yugoslav People's Army lasted from what date to what date?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: From 1971, when I became an active duty-officer, until 1999, when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what rank did you have when you retired?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I was a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that means during 1991 you were in fact an active-duty officer, and that being the case, could you tell us where you were at the time.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I was a lieutenant colonel by rank, and I was the commander of the light artillery division of the anti-aircraft attack in the Radovici barracks, near Tivat. The light artillery battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you were the commander of that unit in Radovici, can you tell me what establishment and unit that unit belonged to?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: It was the 86th Light Artillery --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Battalion which belonged to the 9th Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector, where was that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: It was in Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long you served in the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I served in the 9th Military Naval Sector from 1975 right up until the time I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In 1991, can you tell us who the commander was of the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: In 1991, the commander was warship Captain Djurovic, and after he was killed it was Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know how Commander Krsto Djurovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In a helicopter crash. He died with three other officers. The helicopter crashed and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know who else was with him in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: In the helicopter with him was General Cokic, I think. I think that was his name. And another colonel. I don't know what his name was

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know during that period of time when the accident happened, what General Cokic's duties were? What position did he occupy?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I think he was the Chief of Staff of the 2nd operative group -- Operational Group. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In view of your many years of service in the Military Naval Sector, did Admiral Jokic -- was Admiral Jokic your commander in any other period of time?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before he -- before warship Captain Zec came to command me -- and before him there was another commander; that's true. That would make it in the period from the 1980s, from 1980 to, let's say, 1985, 1986, Jokic was my commander. I can't remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But as an officer, a member of the 9th Military Naval Sector, I'm sure you know Admiral Jokic very well, who, on two occasions, was the commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: At the end of the summer of 1991, I assume you were still at your post at the barracks in Radovici; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for that period of time, when the fighting started on the territory of Dubrovnik and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Well, the fighting started at around the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, were you informed and aware of the situation that the barracks were in, the soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Well, I did know about that from the reporting that took place and information received via the media. I know that the situation was difficult, that they were surrounded, that the barracks were surrounded, along with the soldiers, and that military personnel weren't allowed to move around. They couldn't go and see their families. And they were blocked, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As an officer yourself and as a naval man, do you know whether, in the autumn of 1991 to the end of 1991, the re-dislocation -- resettlement of equipment and materiel, manpower, garrisons took place from the military naval district, from the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And where were they resettled, redeployed, those units?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Mostly they came by naval vessels to the Zelenika port and to the part of Bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So they are ports in Montenegro, are they not?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what about the area in which these soldiers, equipment, and materiel were set up? Did it belong to the 9th Military Naval Sector, where they went to?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: At the beginning of October 1991, where were you yourself? Did you stay on in Radovici or were you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of October, and when the combat operations started, I was in Radovici with my unit, until we received our assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what assignment was that, specifically?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I personally received an assignment from the head of staff of the 9th VPS. I think it was a warship Captain Zec at the time who was the commander. I received my assignment on the telephone to the effect that I should take up the equipment I needed, and the men I needed, and to set off for Grude, where I was to set up a command post, the command of Grude, which I took note of. However, I wasn't quite clear on the assignment, so I contacted Admiral Jokic and asked him to clarify my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, then give me a little more detail. What did the commander Admiral Jokic tell you? What were his explanations? How did he closer determine your assignment in setting up the command post at Grude? What were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: The first and primary task was to try, under the prevailing circumstances, to bring life back to normal, so that the population who stayed on in the area could go back to work normally and that I was supposed to give them all the logistic support needed and do what I could with all the resources, the military resources I had and with all the civilian resources that were not taken up by the war. So that was my primary task.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that with the formation of the command of Grude, setting that up by the Yugoslav People's Army, specifically, in the area of the 9th Military Naval Sector, that the task and assignment was, in fact, to organise civilian life in that place, in that locality, as far as was possible, given the wartime conditions and the combat operations going on round about? Would that be it, in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When you arrived at Grude, what did you come across there? Did you find any of the local inhabitants there?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Most of the local inhabitants of Grude, when I arrived, weren't there. They were in Dubrovnik and Cavtat and other places. They had left Grude. But a small portion of the inhabitants did stay on in their homes, in their houses. They were mostly elderly people. And we gave them what assistance we could. We did our best for them to ensure that they survived, that they should be safe, that nobody should harm them. There was no electricity, no water, so we supplied them with our own power generation system. They ate the food that the soldiers ate. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When you were there, during that period of time, the local inhabitants who had left Grude and gone to Cavtat and Dubrovnik, did they perhaps return to their homes at any time? Did they return to Grude at any time?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: When the fighting stopped and when the command was set up in Cavtat as well, then, through the Red Cross organisation and international organisations which would come to see me, and we discussed the situation, we found a way out, a way in which the population who wished to return to take a look at their houses and properties and land and to do a little work on their land, if need be, we organised transport in trucks from Cavtat to Grude. For example, at around 8.00 in the morning - I can't tell you the exact time, and it varied from one day to the next - up until 1400 hours or 1500 hours in the afternoon we organised this transport and they would go back at that time, in the afternoon, back to the hotels they had been put up in, in Cavtat or Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The local population in Grude, was it given assistance in the form of food supplies and other necessary requirements?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. The basic necessities and what we were able to give them from our wartime reserves. But mostly we were able to supply them with cooked meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: The local population, did they have medical aid and assistance?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Otherwise, in Grude there was a medical centre, a rather large one, and two nurses stayed on who had worked in the medical centre and lived there. They stayed and continued working with our own physician, so that all the necessary medical care and attention was provided to anybody who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me if you remember, you needn't give us the exact number, but do you happen to recall how many soldiers you had under your command in order to meet these needs in Grude?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I arrived with five or six of my men, two officers, and we set all this up. Then I asked General Jokic to allow some of my men who had stayed on in Radovici to come in and assist me and help me organise security and safety for the region, to the sanitation of the terrain and so on, control points and so on. So at Grude, I ended up by having about 20 soldiers and two or three commanding officers during that initial stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between those soldiers and the local inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: It was very proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, how long you stayed in Grude. How long were you there for?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Grude -- or rather, from Grude, I set up the command post at Cavtat, so that afterwards I relinquished my duties to Major Kurdulija, whereas I continued to work in Grude until I received orders from General Jokic, and that was in the second half of November, by which I was supposed to set up a command post in Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 81, it says he received orders from General Jokic. Is he referring to Admiral Jokic or General Strugar or some other general? Could the -- could the transcript be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The order that you received to set up the command at Grude and later on Cavtat and Mokosica, who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether the staff command in Cavtat was founded in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the exact date, but it was around the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On your arrival, when you came to Cavtat, what was the situation there regarding the local population?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Cavtat was mostly untouched, as far as military actions were concerned. The operational army was on the outskirts of Cavtat. The citizens, for the most part, were in their homes, in comparison to Grude and Mokosica, life there was mostly normal, if one can say that. These supplies were much better and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is the reason for that the fact that there were no combat operations in and around Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Because there were no such operations in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the work in order to organise living in Cavtat, to organise the supplies to all the population, in view of the fact that most of the population remained there, was it more difficult to do that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: No. It was much easier to organise that in Cavtat than to do it in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that when the command in Cavtat was formed, after a certain period of time you returned to Grude again. Can you please tell us how long you stayed at the command post in Grude.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until late November, until about the 20th of November, when I was summoned by Admiral Jokic to the forward command post, and he issued me an order to form the staff command in Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say that Admiral Jokic summoned you to the forward command post, can you tell us exactly where this place was located and whose command post it was.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: It was in Kupari, the command post of the 9th VPS, Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you came to Mokosica, what was the situation that you found there?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: When I came to Mokosica, the local population already had formed a crisis staff, their own crisis staff, which was located in a shelter of a building. And together with my communications officer and officer for security, I went there and I told them what my task was, and that from that point on, I was in command of that post, that the staff command should be formed there, which they accepted. And from that point on, we started to work together to set up all of the conditions that I have already mentioned. We started to work to normalise life there. We formed a new crisis staff with some of the people who had already been its members and with the people -- or some of the people that I had brought with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what the situation was with the local population in Mokosica when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Some of the population had fled to Dubrovnik. A larger part remained, according to what Admiral Jokic told me when he gave me this assignment, he told me that there were about 1.600 citizens there, of which about 1.200 were Croats and about 400 were Serbs. He said that a police station was set up with four to six police officers, Croat officers. I was ordered to leave that to function as it had functioned up to that time and that nothing should be changed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you're speaking about the Croat police officers in Mokosica --

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: -- are these members of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these police officers armed?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these police officers carrying their weapons as they were carrying out their duties, while at the same time you, as a representative of the JNA, with your men, were working and living in Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: They did not carry long-barrelled weapons but sidearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there a police station or a police outpost before in Mokosica?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. This is something that was already there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps how Mokosica was taken over by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was the reason for that the fact that you were in Grude before that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Grude prior to that, so that I was not familiar with all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: These Croat police officers who stayed in Mokosica, what did they specifically do? What were their duties?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Their duties were, in cooperation with our military police, to be responsible for the security of the local population, in every way. Various things could have happened. Afterwards, when we organised a regular ferry line between Dubrovnik and Cavtat, we escorted that vessel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when you assumed the command post in Mokosica with the task of organising the civilian life in wartime, who provided you with the necessary personnel in order to carry out this assignment?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: I took some personnel from the Grude command post and transferred them. Then I requested from Admiral Jokic that he should supply a certain number of soldiers, military police officers, to man checkpoints, to deal with security, also preparation of food, supplying of the civilian population, and so on. However, it all boiled down to those people that I had brought with me. Perhaps there was some addition to that. I don't remember exactly how many soldiers arrived. And the military police who had their own duties were not re-subordinated to my command but were under somebody else's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know which MP unit is that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: That was the military police from the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct if I say that because of the different circumstances and objective circumstances in that area, you had certain problems related to a shortage of personnel in order to be able to carry out the tasks you were required to?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: While you were in Mokosica, were there any provocations there from the other side, from the Croat side? I am thinking about fire provocations, firing provocations.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Geographically speaking, my command post was on the opposite bank of the Rijeka Dubrovacka, at a distance of 250 to 300 metres, so that you could open fire from infantry weapons. So there were some provocations, mostly on the road from Mokosica to the -- I cannot remember the name at the moment. I cannot remember the name. But mostly also at the motor vehicles which were used for food supplies, also to bring in water, or Red Cross vehicles which were marked appropriately. Fire was opened at those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The Croat side, did they open fire at these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to show the witness map Exhibit P132.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurasic --

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: -- could you please open the map to the place where you can see Mokosica and this area that you were talking about, and could you fold it and then place it on the ELMO, please. Could we please zoom in so that we can see better. Could we go a little more to the left, please, so that we could see what the witness is pointing to. This part of the sea that is going in to land, cutting into the land, what is the name of that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: That is Rijeka Dubrovacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where Mokosica is.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: This is Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is the Mokosica staff command indicated here on this map?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please point to it with the pointer -- where it states staff command?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO DJURASIC
utterances.text: That's correct

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt. We have the French interpretation from English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is the English interpretation okay now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I hear an English-speaking voice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we already -- also had certain problems with the transcript, I would like to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurasic, you pointed out the Mokosica staff command. My question was: What is the settlement which was opposite from you?
